title: Unknown extensions
text:
Every lookup returns something. That is convenient right up to the moment you need to know whether the answer was a confident match or a shrug. This page is about telling the two apart, and about what to do once you can.

The shrug looks like an answer
get_content_type() returns a string unless you ask it not to. For a known extension the string is the content type. For an unknown one it is a fallback, and the default fallback is application/octet-stream.
import content_types

content_types.get_content_type('data.parquet')  # 'application/vnd.apache.parquet'
content_types.get_content_type('notes.xyz')  # 'application/octet-stream'
content_types.get_content_type('Makefile')  # 'application/octet-stream'
application/octet-stream is a perfectly good header. It is what S3 and most web servers send when they do not know better, and browsers respond by offering a download, which is the safe move for mystery bytes. The trouble is that it is also a real answer. A handful of formats genuinely map to it, on purpose, because there is no better registered type: .bin, .pkl, .npy, .so, .o, and a few more. So when you see application/octet-stream come back, you cannot tell from the string alone whether the table recognised the extension or gave up.
Think of it as a detective who, when stumped, writes “unknown substance” on the report. Useful, as long as you remember that some substances really are labelled “unknown substance”.


Three ways to handle a miss
Change the shrug. If the files you deal with are mostly text, tell the lookup to shrug in the other direction. treat_as_binary=False swaps the default fallback for text/plain.
content_types.get_content_type('notes.xyz', treat_as_binary=False)  # 'text/plain'
Write your own shrug. Pass any string as fallback and that is what comes back for every unknown extension. It outranks treat_as_binary. Known extensions are untouched.
content_types.get_content_type('notes.xyz', fallback='application/x-acme')  # 'application/x-acme'
content_types.get_content_type('photo.jpg', fallback='application/x-acme')  # 'image/jpeg'
Refuse to shrug. Pass fallback=None and a miss comes back as None. Now you can branch. This is the mode to use when a miss should change what the program does next, for example to hand the file to a byte-sniffing library, to reject the upload, or to log it for a human.
content_type = content_types.get_content_type(name, fallback=None)
if content_type is None:
    content_type = sniff_with_python_magic(path)
One subtlety that bites people who skim: leaving fallback out and passing fallback=None are different things. Leaving it out keeps the historical default. The parameter’s real default is a private sentinel, precisely so that an explicit None can mean “give me None” without changing behaviour for every caller who never passes the argument. Your type checker knows this too. The plain call types as str, and only fallback=None widens it to Optional[str].


Ask the table directly
If you only want a yes or a no, skip the function and ask the table. Keys are bare lowercase extensions with no leading dot.
ext = 'parquet'
ext in content_types.EXTENSION_TO_CONTENT_TYPE  # True


Teaching it a new word
The table is a plain dict, and the forward lookup reads it fresh on every call, so an addition takes effect immediately. Keys must be lowercase and have no leading dot.
content_types.EXTENSION_TO_CONTENT_TYPE['acme'] = 'application/x-acme'
content_types.get_content_type('report.acme')  # 'application/x-acme'
Do this once at startup, not inside a request handler. And do it before the first reverse lookup, because guess_extension() builds its inverted view of the table on first use and caches it for the life of the process. Additions made after that are visible to the forward lookup but invisible to the reverse one.
If the extension is a real, widely used format that other people would reasonably expect to work, do not keep the fix to yourself. Open an issue or send a pull request and it ends up in the table for everyone.


Things that look like misses but are not

None as the filename raises TypeError. That is a bug in the caller, not an unknown extension, and the library refuses to paper over it.
archive.tar.gz returns application/gzip. That is a hit on the last segment, and it is the correct type for the compressed container.

And things that are misses, in case you were wondering: an empty string, a name with no dot anywhere, and a URL with no file component such as https://example.com/download. All three get the fallback.

title: Getting started
text:
Imagine someone hands you a sealed envelope and asks what is inside. You are not allowed to open it. All you get is the label on the front. That is the job content-types does, and it turns out the label is usually enough.

The envelope problem
Here is how the problem shows up in real code. You have a bucket in S3 with a few hundred thousand objects. A customer’s browser asks for one of them, and your job is to send back a Content-Type header so the browser knows whether to render an image, play audio, or offer a download. The honest way to find out is to fetch the object and look at its first few bytes. The honest way is also slow, costs money, and is silly when the key already says invoice-2026-03.pdf.
The same situation shows up when you are uploading. S3 will happily store report.pdf as binary/octet-stream if you let it, and then every link to that file becomes a download instead of a tab. You want to set the type correctly at upload time, and again, you already know the filename.
content-types answers the question from the label. It takes the extension, looks it up in a table of 364 entries, and returns the type. It never opens, reads, or sniffs anything, so it is safe to call on names of files that live on another machine, on URLs you have not fetched, and on files that do not exist yet.


Install
Requires Python 3.10 or later. There are no runtime dependencies, so it adds nothing to your lock file but itself.
uv add content-types
# or
pip install content-types


The first lookup
import content_types

content_types.get_content_type('report.pdf')
# 'application/pdf'
That is the whole core API. One function, one string in, one string out. The import name is content_types with an underscore; the distribution and the command line tool are content-types with a hyphen. Python cannot import a hyphen, so the two spellings are a fact of life.


It is not fussy about what you hand it
The function was written by someone who got tired of normalising filenames before every call, so it does the normalising for you. A full path, a bare extension with or without the dot, a pathlib.Path, or a URL all work, and case does not matter.
from pathlib import Path

content_types.get_content_type('photo.JPG')  # 'image/jpeg'
content_types.get_content_type('images/photo.jpg')  # 'image/jpeg'
content_types.get_content_type('jpg')  # 'image/jpeg'
content_types.get_content_type('.jpg')  # 'image/jpeg'
content_types.get_content_type(Path('/data/photo.jpg'))  # 'image/jpeg'
content_types.get_content_type('https://cdn.example.com/a.mp3?v=3#t=10')  # 'audio/mpeg'
Three details are worth knowing up front, because each one has surprised someone.

For URLs, the query string and the fragment are thrown away before the lookup. A cache-busting ?v=3 does not turn your MP3 into a mystery.
For compound extensions the last segment wins. archive.tar.gz resolves as gz and returns application/gzip, which is the right answer for the outer container. There is no special knowledge of .tar.gz as a unit.
Dotfiles such as .env and .gitignore are in the table and resolve to text/plain. They are extensions with no name in front, and the lookup treats them that way.



When the label is blank
Sometimes the envelope says Makefile, or notes.xyz, or nothing at all. For those the function returns application/octet-stream, the universal “it is bytes, I cannot tell you more” type. That is the correct thing to put in a header, but it is not always what you want in your own logic, and it hides the fact that a lookup missed. The next page, Unknown extensions, is about telling a miss from a hit and deciding what to do about it.


Shortcut constants
For a handful of formats you reach for daily, the module hands you the answer as a plain string so you do not even write the call.
content_types.json  # 'application/json'
content_types.pdf  # 'application/pdf'
content_types.parquet  # 'application/vnd.apache.parquet'
The full set is webp, png, jpg, mp3, json, pdf, zip, xml, csv, md, parquet, ipynb, pkl, yaml, toml, and sqlite. One caution: write import content_types and use attribute access. from content_types import json quietly shadows the standard library json module, and you will spend an unhappy afternoon wondering why json.loads is a string.


Where to go next

Unknown extensions is the detective work: telling a miss from a hit and the three ways to handle one.
Reverse lookup runs the envelope backwards, from a content type or a Content-Type header to an extension.
Command line covers the content-types tool for quick answers in a shell.
Compared to mimetypes explains why the standard library was not enough and how the table differs.
FAQ collects the questions people actually ask.
The API reference lists every public name with its signature.

title: Compared to mimetypes
text:
Python already ships a mimetypes module, and the first question anyone sensible asks is why this library exists at all. The short answer is that mimetypes was tried first and came up short in two different ways. The longer answer is this page.

How the lookup works
There is no magic to describe, and that is the point. Everything is one dictionary, EXTENSION_TO_CONTENT_TYPE, with 364 bare lowercase extensions as keys. get_content_type() trims its input down to the last dot-separated segment, lowercases it, and reads the dictionary. The reverse functions invert that same dictionary the first time they are called and cache the result for the life of the process. Nothing is read from disk, no system mime.types file is consulted, and the answers are identical on every operating system and every Python version. Same input, same output, forever.


The two problems with the standard library
It depends on which Python you are running. The built-in table in mimetypes has 142 entries on Python 3.10. By Python 3.15 it has grown to about 210. That growth is good news, but it means the answer to “what type is .yaml” changes with your interpreter: on 3.15 the standard library knows, and on 3.12 it returns None. Between 170 and 220 of this library’s extensions are missing from mimetypes, depending on the version. Some are missing on every supported Python: .tgz, .parquet, .ipynb, .rs, .go, .tsx, .psd, and .dwg among them. Others, such as .yaml, .toml, .webp, .flac, .epub, and .mkv, were added in recent releases, so code that works on a developer’s laptop can fail quietly on an older production image.
Some of its answers are out of date. mimetypes still returns text/xml for .xml, where MDN and current practice say application/xml. This library standardises on the modern type and keeps the old spelling as an alias on reverse lookup, so you are never stranded by a server that sends the legacy form. The other deliberate choices follow the same logic: .js is text/javascript, .yaml and .yml are application/yaml per RFC 9512, and .md is text/markdown.


The API is not the same either
Do not guess this library’s API from the standard library’s. get_content_type() returns one string, not the (type, encoding) tuple that mimetypes.guess_type() returns, and it never hands you None unless you ask for that with fallback=None. The reverse functions keep the familiar names, guess_extension() and guess_all_extensions(), but they accept raw header values with parameters, resolve legacy aliases, and can choose a different canonical extension, for example .html for text/html where the standard library often says .htm.
If you want to see the exact differences on your own interpreter rather than take this page’s word for it, the repository includes a script that prints them.
uv run python samples/compare_to_builtin.py


Why not python-magic
python-magic and its relatives identify a file by reading its leading bytes. When you have the bytes, that is the more reliable method, and it is the only method that works when the extension is missing or lying. This library exists for the other case: you know the name but not the contents. An object key in S3, a URL you have not fetched, a filename in a form submission. The two are not rivals. fallback=None is the hook for handing a miss over to byte sniffing, as shown in Unknown extensions.


What is in the table
The 364 entries cover more ground than you would expect from a MIME table. Images including a dozen camera RAW formats. Audio and video from MP3 to DSD to Matroska. Archives and the newer compression formats such as zstd and brotli. Office and OpenDocument files. Source code for around thirty languages. Data science formats such as Parquet, Arrow, HDF5, pickle, NumPy, R, Stata, SAS, and SPSS. Configuration and infrastructure files, Adobe and CAD formats, game engine assets, scientific formats such as FITS, DICOM, and NIfTI, and subtitle files. The reference page lists every one.

# content-types

You know a filename, an S3 key, or a URL and need its MIME type without downloading or opening anything. `content_types.get_content_type()` returns the type string for the extension, or `application/octet-stream` when the extension is unknown. `guess_extension()` goes the other way, from a type or header value to an extension. Nothing here reads bytes. The import name is `content_types`; the distribution and CLI name is `content-types`.

## Install

```bash
uv add content-types        # or: pip install content-types
```

## Use

```python
import content_types

content_types.get_content_type('report.pdf')  # 'application/pdf'
content_types.get_content_type('https://cdn.x.com/a.mp3?v=3')  # 'audio/mpeg', query stripped
content_types.get_content_type('notes.xyz', fallback=None)  # None, so you can branch on a miss
content_types.guess_extension('text/html; charset=utf-8')  # '.html', params ignored
```

S3 upload: `ExtraArgs={'ContentType': content_types.get_content_type(key)}`. Download naming: `ext = content_types.guess_extension(resp.headers['content-type']) or '.bin'`.

## Rules

- Lookup only. The file does not need to exist and is never opened. For byte sniffing use another tool and fall through to it on `fallback=None`.
- Unknown extensions return `application/octet-stream`, not `None`, so a miss looks like a hit. Some real formats (`.bin`, `.pkl`, `.npy`, `.so`) also map to that type on purpose. Pass `fallback=None` when you need to know.
- `fallback` beats `treat_as_binary`. Omitting `fallback` and passing `fallback=None` are different: the default is a private sentinel, so omitting it keeps the `application/octet-stream` / `text/plain` behaviour.
- Typing: the default call and a string `fallback` return `str`; only `fallback=None` returns `Optional[str]`. Overloads make this precise, so do not add needless `assert x is not None` after a default call.
- The last dot-segment wins. `archive.tar.gz` is `application/gzip`; there is no `tar.gz` entry. `.env` and `.gitignore` are known and return `text/plain`. `Makefile`, `''`, and a URL with no file part are misses.
- Matching is case-insensitive both directions. `?query` and `#fragment` are stripped from URLs first.
- `None` as the input raises `TypeError` in every function. Unknown values do not raise anywhere: forward gives the fallback, `guess_extension` gives `None`, `guess_all_extensions` gives `[]`.
- Reverse lookup accepts raw header values with parameters and legacy spellings (`text/json`, `image/jpg`, `audio/mp3`, `text/xml`, `application/javascript`, `application/x-yaml`, `application/x-zip-compressed`, `application/x-gzip`). Canonical picks differ from stdlib: `text/html` gives `.html`, `image/jpeg` gives `.jpg`, `image/tiff` gives `.tiff`. `guess_extension(t) == guess_all_extensions(t)[0]` always.
- The answers are deliberately modern and differ from `mimetypes`: `.xml` is `application/xml`, `.js` is `text/javascript`, `.yaml` / `.yml` are `application/yaml` (RFC 9512), `.md` is `text/markdown`. Do not "correct" them back.
- The API is not `mimetypes`. There is no `guess_type()`; the forward call is `get_content_type()` and it returns one string, not a `(type, encoding)` tuple.
- `EXTENSION_TO_CONTENT_TYPE` keys have no leading dot (`['jpg']`, never `['.jpg']`). It is a plain dict and may be extended at startup; the reverse map is built once on first reverse call and cached, so add entries before that.
- Prefer `import content_types` and attribute access. `from content_types import json, csv, zip` shadows a stdlib module, a stdlib module, and a builtin.
- Second calls are plain dict reads. There is no state, no config, and no environment variable.

## Decision table

| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Header or S3 ContentType for a name you have | `get_content_type(name)` |
| Know whether the extension is unknown | `get_content_type(name, fallback=None)` and test for `None` |
| Text default instead of binary for misses | `get_content_type(name, treat_as_binary=False)` |
| Your own placeholder for misses | `get_content_type(name, fallback='application/x-acme')` |
| Extension for a `Content-Type` header value | `guess_extension(header)` then `or` a default |
| Every extension for a type, canonical first | `guess_all_extensions(content_type)` |
| Bare extension without the dot | `with_dot=False` on either reverse function |
| Yes/no membership with no fallback | `ext in EXTENSION_TO_CONTENT_TYPE` (lowercase, no dot) |
| Common type without a call | `content_types.json`, `.pdf`, `.png`, `.parquet`, ... |
| Shell one-off | `content-types photo.jpg` |

## API

- `get_content_type(filename_or_extension: str | Path, treat_as_binary: bool = True, fallback: str | None = <omitted>) -> str` (`Optional[str]` only with `fallback=None`). Raises `TypeError` on `None` input. Forward lookup; this is the one you want most of the time.
- `guess_extension(content_type: str, with_dot: bool = True) -> Optional[str]`. Raises `TypeError` on `None`. Returns the canonical extension or `None`.
- `guess_all_extensions(content_type: str, with_dot: bool = True) -> list[str]`. Raises `TypeError` on `None`. Returns all extensions canonical first, or `[]`.
- `EXTENSION_TO_CONTENT_TYPE: dict[str, str]`. 364 bare-extension keys. The single source of truth for both directions.
- Constants `webp png jpg mp3 json pdf zip xml csv md parquet ipynb pkl yaml toml sqlite: str`. Plain strings computed at import.
- `cli() -> None`. Entry point for the `content-types` script. One positional argument, forward lookup only; `-h` / `--help` and `--version` exit 0; no argument prints usage and exits 1; unknown extension prints `application/octet-stream` and exits 0.

## Worked example

```python
>>> content_types.get_content_type('model.pkl')
'application/octet-stream'      # a hit: .pkl really is octet-stream
>>> content_types.get_content_type('model.pkl', fallback=None)
'application/octet-stream'      # still a string, so the extension is known
>>> content_types.get_content_type('model.weights', fallback=None)
None                            # a miss: not in the table
>>> content_types.guess_all_extensions('application/octet-stream')[:3]
['.bin', '.a', '.so']           # reverse of a catch-all type is a guess at best
```

Fix order on a miss: check the spelling and case of the name, check `EXTENSION_TO_CONTENT_TYPE` for the bare key, add the entry at startup if it is private to your app, and open an issue at the repo if it is a format others would expect.

title: API Reference
text:
content-types is intentionally tiny: lookup functions for both directions (filename -> type, and type -> extension), the mapping table behind them, and a handful of precomputed shortcut constants for the most common formats.


Forward lookup

Map a filename, bare extension, Path, or URL to its MIME / content type.


get_content_type()

Return the most specific, commonly accepted MIME type for a filename or extension.




Reverse lookup

Map a MIME / content type back to its file extension(s) — the inverse of get_content_type.


guess_extension()

Return the canonical file extension for a MIME / content type.

guess_all_extensions()

Return every known file extension for a MIME / content type, canonical first.




Mapping data

The underlying extension -> content-type table (364 entries; keys have no leading dot).


EXTENSION_TO_CONTENT_TYPE

The extension -> content type table that every lookup reads from.




Shortcut constants

Precomputed content types for very common formats, exposed as module-level attributes.


webp

The content type for .webp files: image/webp.

png

The content type for .png files: image/png.

jpg

The content type for .jpg files: image/jpeg.

mp3

The content type for .mp3 files: audio/mpeg.

json

The content type for .json files: application/json.

The content type for .pdf files: application/pdf.

The content type for .zip files: application/zip.

The content type for .xml files: application/xml.

The content type for .csv files: text/csv.

title: guess_all_extensions()
text:
Return every known file extension for a MIME / content type, canonical first.


Usage
Source


guess_all_extensions(content_type, with_dot=True)


Like guess_extension(), but returns the full list rather than just the canonical extension. The lookup is case-insensitive, MIME parameters are ignored, and common non-canonical spellings (e.g. text/json, image/jpg) resolve to their canonical type. The first element always equals guess_extension(content_type). The order follows this library’s table (canonical first) and is not guaranteed to match the standard library mimetypes module.


Parameters


content_type: str

A MIME type to look up, optionally with parameters (e.g. image/jpeg or text/html; charset=utf-8).

with_dot: bool = True

When True (default) each extension has a leading dot (e.g. .jpg); when False the bare extensions are returned (e.g. jpg).





Returns


 list[str]

A list of extensions, canonical first, or an empty list if the content type is
unknown (including empty, whitespace-only, or parameter-only input).





Raises


 TypeError

If content_type is None.





Example
>>> guess_all_extensions("image/jpeg")
['.jpg', '.jpeg', '.jpe']
>>> guess_all_extensions("text/html")
['.html', '.htm']
>>> guess_all_extensions("application/pdf")
['.pdf']
>>> guess_all_extensions("application/x-does-not-exist")
[]

Extensive Format Support
With 360+ file extensions mapped, content-types covers:

🎨 Images - Standard formats plus RAW camera files (Canon, Nikon, Sony, Adobe DNG, etc.)
🎵 Audio - MP3, FLAC, AAC, MIDI, WMA, ALAC, DSD, and more

title: content-types 🗃️🔎
text:
Usage
import content_types

# Forward lookup: filename -> MIME type
the_type = content_types.get_content_type('example.jpg')
print(the_type)  # 'image/jpeg'

# Works with any supported extension
print(content_types.get_content_type('data.parquet'))  # 'application/vnd.apache.parquet'
print(content_types.get_content_type('notebook.ipynb'))  # 'application/x-ipynb+json'
print(content_types.get_content_type('photo.cr2'))  # 'image/x-canon-cr2'
print(content_types.get_content_type('model.blend'))  # 'application/x-blender'
print(content_types.get_content_type('contract.sol'))  # 'text/x-solidity'

# For very common files, you have shortcuts:
print(f'Content-Type for webp is {content_types.webp}.')
# Content-Type for webp is image/webp.

# Data science shortcuts
print(content_types.parquet)  # 'application/vnd.apache.parquet'
print(content_types.ipynb)  # 'application/x-ipynb+json'
print(content_types.pkl)  # 'application/octet-stream'
print(content_types.yaml)  # 'application/yaml'
print(content_types.toml)  # 'application/toml'
print(content_types.sqlite)  # 'application/vnd.sqlite3'

# Works with Path objects too
from pathlib import Path

path = Path('document.pdf')
print(content_types.get_content_type(path))  # 'application/pdf'

# URLs work too: query strings and fragments are stripped before lookup
url = 'https://cdn.example.com/song.mp3?cache_id=678c2a'
print(content_types.get_content_type(url))  # 'audio/mpeg'

# Unknown extensions fall back to 'application/octet-stream' by default;
# pass treat_as_binary=False to fall back to 'text/plain' instead.
print(content_types.get_content_type('notes.unknownext'))  # 'application/octet-stream'
print(content_types.get_content_type('notes.unknownext', treat_as_binary=False))  # 'text/plain'

# Or supply your own fallback for unknown extensions; it takes precedence
# over treat_as_binary. Known extensions still resolve normally.
print(content_types.get_content_type('notes.unknownext', fallback='application/x-custom'))  # 'application/x-custom'

# Pass fallback=None to get None back for unknowns (e.g. to branch on a miss).
# Omitting fallback keeps the default 'application/octet-stream', so existing callers are unaffected.
print(content_types.get_content_type('notes.unknownext', fallback=None))  # None
print(content_types.get_content_type('photo.jpg', fallback=None))  # 'image/jpeg' (known, unaffected)

# Reverse lookup: MIME type -> extension (the inverse of get_content_type)
print(content_types.guess_extension('application/pdf'))  # '.pdf'
print(content_types.guess_extension('image/jpeg'))  # '.jpg' (the canonical pick)
print(content_types.guess_all_extensions('image/jpeg'))  # ['.jpg', '.jpeg', '.jpe']

# Matching is case-insensitive, and parameters on a Content-Type header are ignored
print(content_types.guess_extension('text/html; charset=utf-8'))  # '.html'

# Common non-canonical / legacy spellings resolve to the canonical type too
print(content_types.guess_extension('text/json'))  # '.json'  (canonical: application/json)
print(content_types.guess_extension('image/jpg'))  # '.jpg'   (canonical: image/jpeg)

# Pass with_dot=False for a bare extension; unknown types return None / []
print(content_types.guess_extension('application/toml', with_dot=False))  # 'toml'
print(content_types.guess_extension('application/x-nope'))  # None
print(content_types.guess_all_extensions('application/x-nope'))  # []
The reverse lookup mirrors the standard library mimetypes.guess_extension / guess_all_extensions, but draws on this library’s larger, more-correct table, so the canonical extension can differ (for example, it returns .html for text/html, not .htm). It is also forgiving of common non-canonical spellings: text/json, image/jpg, application/javascript, and application/x-zip-compressed all resolve to a sensible extension. See Reverse lookup for the details.
The type checker sees str for the default call and for a string fallback; only an explicit fallback=None widens the return type to Optional[str]. For the full story on misses, see Unknown extensions.

CLI
To use the library as a CLI tool, just install it with uv or pipx.
uv tool install content-types
Now it will be available machine-wide.

title: content-types 🗃️🔎
text:
More correct than Python’s mimetypes
When I first learned about Python’s mimetypes module, I thought it was exactly what I need. However, it doesn’t have all the MIME types, and it recommends deprecated, out-of-date answers for very obvious types.
For example, mimetypes has .xml as text/xml where it should be application/xml (see MDN).
Its coverage also depends on which Python you run. The built-in table has 142 entries on Python 3.10 and about 210 on Python 3.15, so an extension that resolves on one interpreter can come back None on another. Types missing from mimetypes on every supported Python include:

.tgz -> application/gzip
.parquet -> application/vnd.apache.parquet
.ipynb -> application/x-ipynb+json
.rs -> text/x-rust
.go -> text/x-go
.tsx -> text/tsx
.psd -> image/vnd.adobe.photoshop
.dwg -> application/acad
… and 170 to 220 more, depending on your Python version

Older Pythons are also missing everyday types such as .webp, .yaml, .toml, .flac, .epub, and .mkv that newer releases have since added. With this library, you get 360+ file extensions properly mapped, with the same answers on every Python version. See Compared to mimetypes for how the lookup works and a script that prints the exact differences on your interpreter.

title: content-types 🗃️🔎
text:
Works when python-magic package doesn’t
Why not the excellent python-magic package? That one works by reading the header bytes of binary files which requires access to the file data. The whole goal of this project is to avoid accessing or needing the file data. They are for different use-cases, and fallback=None is the hook for falling through to byte sniffing when the extension is unknown.

title: get_content_type()
text:
Return the most specific, commonly accepted MIME type for a filename or extension.


Usage
Source


get_content_type(filename_or_extension: str | Path, treat_as_binary: bool = True, fallback: str | _Unset = _UNSET) -> str
get_content_type(filename_or_extension: str | Path, treat_as_binary: bool = True, fallback: None) -> Optional[str]
get_content_type(filename_or_extension: str | Path, treat_as_binary: bool, fallback: None) -> Optional[str]


The lookup is based purely on the extension — the file’s bytes are never read. A filename, a bare extension (with or without a leading dot), or a pathlib.Path are all accepted. For URLs, any query string (?...) or fragment (#...) is stripped first; for compound extensions the last segment wins (archive.tar.gz resolves as gz). Matching is case-insensitive.


Parameters


filename_or_extension: str | Path

A filename, path, URL, or bare extension to look up. Accepts a str or a pathlib.Path.

treat_as_binary: bool = True

Selects the default fallback when the extension is unknown and no explicit fallback is given. True (default) returns application/octet-stream; False returns text/plain.

fallback: Optional[str] | _Unset = _UNSET

An explicit value to return for unknown extensions. When provided, it takes precedence over treat_as_binary. Pass a MIME type string to override the default, or None to get None back for unknowns (handy when you want to branch on a miss rather than receive a placeholder type). When omitted entirely, the treat_as_binary default is used — so existing callers are unaffected.





Returns


 Optional[str]

For a known extension, its MIME type; otherwise the explicit fallback (which may be None) or the default.





Raises


 TypeError

If filename_or_extension is None.





Example
>>> get_content_type("picture.jpg")
'image/jpeg'
>>> get_content_type(".webp")
'image/webp'
>>> get_content_type("script.js")
'text/javascript'
>>> get_content_type("unknown.xyz")
'application/octet-stream'
>>> get_content_type("unknown.xyz", treat_as_binary=False)
'text/plain'
>>> get_content_type("unknown.xyz", fallback='application/x-custom')
'application/x-custom'
>>> get_content_type("unknown.xyz", fallback=None) is None
True

title: guess_extension()
text:
Return the canonical file extension for a MIME / content type.


Usage
Source


guess_extension(content_type, with_dot=True)


This is the reverse of get_content_type(). The lookup is case-insensitive and any MIME parameters are ignored, so an HTTP Content-Type header value such as text/html; charset=utf-8 resolves the same as text/html. Common non-canonical or legacy spellings are also accepted — text/json resolves like application/json and image/jpg like image/jpeg. When a content type maps to several extensions, the canonical one is returned (e.g. image/jpeg -> .jpg); use guess_all_extensions() to get every extension.
The canonical choice follows this library’s table and may differ from the standard library mimetypes module — for example, this returns .html for text/html.


Parameters


content_type: str

A MIME type to look up, optionally with parameters (e.g. application/pdf or text/html; charset=utf-8).

with_dot: bool = True

When True (default) the returned extension has a leading dot (e.g. .pdf), which is what you concatenate onto a filename. When False the bare extension is returned (e.g. pdf).





Returns


 Optional[str]

The canonical extension for the content type, or None if it is unknown
(including empty, whitespace-only, or parameter-only input).





Raises


 TypeError

If content_type is None.





Example
>>> guess_extension("application/pdf")
'.pdf'
>>> guess_extension("image/jpeg")
'.jpg'
>>> guess_extension("text/html; charset=utf-8")
'.html'
>>> guess_extension("application/pdf", with_dot=False)
'pdf'
>>> guess_extension("application/x-does-not-exist") is None
True

title: Command line
text:
Sometimes the question is not in your code at all. You are staring at a bucket listing, or a log line, or a colleague’s message, and you want to know what report.parq is going to be served as without opening a REPL. The package ships a small console script for exactly that moment.

Install
Install it as a tool so it is on your path everywhere.
uv tool install content-types
# or
pipx install content-types
Inside a project that already depends on the package the script is on the virtualenv’s path, so uv run content-types ... works there without a separate install.


Use
One argument in, one line out.
content-types example.jpg
# image/jpeg

content-types .webp
# image/webp

content-types data.parquet
# application/vnd.apache.parquet
The argument goes straight through get_content_type() with its defaults, so the tool inherits the library’s manners: case does not matter, a bare extension works with or without the dot, and an unknown extension prints application/octet-stream and exits 0. It does the forward lookup only. For the reverse direction, open Python.


Flags and exit codes
The script is deliberately tiny, so this table is the whole contract.








Invocation
Output
Exit code




content-types NAME
the content type, or application/octet-stream for an unknown extension
0


content-types
usage text on stdout
1


content-types -h or --help
usage text
0


content-types --version
the installed package version
0



Extra arguments after the first are ignored. There are no environment variables and no configuration file to discover. Under the hood the script is the function content_types.cli() wired up in pyproject.toml, which means you can call it yourself if you ever want the same behaviour from inside another tool.

title: FAQ
text:
The questions that actually get asked, with short answers and a pointer to the page that goes deeper.

Does it read the file?
No, never. Every function works from the name alone. The file does not have to exist, and nothing is opened. If you need byte-level detection, use a sniffing library and fall through to it on a miss as shown in Unknown extensions.


Why did I get application/octet-stream?
One of two reasons. Either the extension is not in the table, or it is one of the formats that honestly map to that type, such as .bin, .pkl, or .npy. To tell them apart, pass fallback=None: a real entry still returns the string, and a miss returns None.


Is .tar.gz handled as a unit?
No. The last segment wins, so archive.tar.gz returns application/gzip, which is the correct type for the compressed container you are actually holding. There is no special casing for double extensions.


Does it care about case?
No. Extensions are lowercased before the lookup, and content types are lowercased in the reverse direction. PHOTO.JPG and IMAGE/JPEG both work.


Does it handle URLs?
Yes. Query strings and fragments are stripped before the lookup, so https://cdn.example.com/a.mp3?v=3 returns audio/mpeg. A URL with no file component, such as https://example.com/download, is a miss.


Why do my Path and string results disagree for dotfiles?
They should not. Both Path('.env') and the string '.env' return text/plain. Releases before the next one used Path.suffix, which is empty for a dotfile, so the Path form quietly fell through to the fallback. That is fixed.


The type checker says get_content_type() returns Optional[str]
It returns str unless you pass fallback=None. The function is overloaded so that the default call and a string fallback type as str, and only an explicit fallback=None types as Optional[str]. If your checker still shows the wider type everywhere, you are on a release before the next one.


Can I add or override an extension?
Yes. Assign into content_types.EXTENSION_TO_CONTENT_TYPE with a bare lowercase key. Do it at startup and before the first reverse lookup, because the reverse map is built once and cached. For formats other people would expect to work, open an issue so the table is fixed for everyone.


Why does guess_extension('text/html') return .html and not .htm?
Because .html is what people write today, and .htm is a leftover from eight-character filenames. The library keeps a short list of canonical overrides for cases like this. The standard library makes different choices, so do not expect the two to agree.


What about text/yaml or application/x-yaml?
The forward direction returns application/yaml for .yaml and .yml, following RFC 9512. The reverse direction accepts the legacy spellings as aliases and returns .yaml.


Is it thread-safe?
Yes for reads, which is all most programs do. The forward lookup is a dictionary read and the reverse map is built with functools.cache. If you mutate the table, do it at startup before spawning threads.


How do I run the tests?
uv run --with pytest pytest
See the README for lint and docs commands.

title: Reverse lookup
text:
So far the envelope has had a label and you wanted to know what was inside. Now flip it. A server has just told you what is inside, in the form of a Content-Type header, and you need to write a label. That is reverse lookup, and it is harder than it sounds.

From a type to an extension
guess_extension() is the inverse of get_content_type(). Give it a content type and it returns the canonical extension, with the dot, ready to append to a filename. guess_all_extensions() returns every extension known for that type, canonical first.
import content_types

content_types.guess_extension('application/pdf')  # '.pdf'
content_types.guess_extension('image/jpeg')  # '.jpg'
content_types.guess_all_extensions('image/jpeg')  # ['.jpg', '.jpeg', '.jpe']
content_types.guess_extension('image/jpeg', with_dot=False)  # 'jpg'
The classic use is naming a download when the URL gives you nothing to go on.
import httpx
from pathlib import Path

resp = httpx.get('https://example.com/download/item')
ext = content_types.guess_extension(resp.headers['content-type'])
if ext:
    Path(f'downloaded{ext}').write_bytes(resp.content)


Why the reverse direction is the hard one
The forward table is one-to-one. Each of its 364 extensions maps to exactly one type. Run it backwards and it is one-to-many: those 364 extensions collapse onto 223 types, and 57 of those types have more than one extension pointing at them. image/jpeg is claimed by .jpg, .jpeg, and .jpe. Which one do you write on the label? Someone has to pick, and the pick has to be stable.
The rule is that the first extension listed for a type in EXTENSION_TO_CONTENT_TYPE wins, with a short list of deliberate overrides where the first-listed spelling is the one nobody uses any more: text/html gives .html not .htm, image/tiff gives .tiff, video/mpeg gives .mpeg, and application/x-msdownload gives .exe rather than .dll. Whatever the pick, guess_extension(t) is always equal to guess_all_extensions(t)[0], and a test enforces it.
The standard library makes its own picks and orders its lists differently, so do not expect the two to agree. Compared to mimetypes has the details.


It reads headers as servers actually write them
Real Content-Type headers are messy. They carry parameters, they vary in case, and a surprising number of servers send spellings that were never registered. The reverse lookup takes all of that in stride.

Case is ignored. IMAGE/JPEG resolves like image/jpeg.
Parameters are stripped, so you can pass the raw header value. text/html; charset=utf-8 resolves like text/html.
Legacy and mistaken spellings resolve to the type this library uses. text/json, image/jpg, audio/mp3, text/xml, application/javascript, application/x-yaml, application/x-zip-compressed, and application/x-gzip all work. The complete alias list lives in the source as _CONTENT_TYPE_ALIASES, and tests check that every alias points at a real type and never shadows one.



When it does not know
An unknown content type is not an error. guess_extension() returns None and guess_all_extensions() returns []. Empty, whitespace-only, and parameter-only input all count as unknown. Passing None raises TypeError, matching the forward function.
content_types.guess_extension('application/x-nope')  # None
content_types.guess_all_extensions('application/x-nope')  # []
The or idiom is your friend here: guess_extension(header) or '.bin' gives you a usable label every time.


The two catch-all types
text/plain and application/octet-stream are where extensions go when nothing more specific exists. text/plain has 32 extensions in the table and application/octet-stream has 24. Asked for the canonical pick, the library gives you .txt and .bin, which is as sensible as it gets. Asked for the full list, it gives you config files, pickles, object files, and database fragments all in one pile. If a server tells you application/octet-stream, the honest reading is that it does not know either, and any extension you write is a guess.
